content: Heart disease is a broad term encompassing various conditions that affect the heart. As of 2007, it remains the leading cause of death in the United States. Types of Heart Disease Cardiomyopathy Cardiomyopathy refers to diseases of the heart muscle itself. Individuals with cardiomyopathy are at increased risk of arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. Extrinsic Cardiomyopathies: These are caused by factors outside the myocardium. The most common cause is ischemia. Examples include: Alcoholic cardiomyopathy Coronary artery disease Congenital heart disease Nutritional diseases affecting the heart Ischemic cardiomyopathy Hypertensive cardiomyopathy Valvular cardiomyopathy Inflammatory cardiomyopathy Cardiomyopathy secondary to systemic metabolic disease Intrinsic Cardiomyopathies: These involve weakness in the heart muscle not attributable to external causes. Types include: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM): The most common form, often leading to heart transplantation. It is characterized by an enlarged heart, particularly the left ventricle, with reduced pumping function. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM or HOCM): A genetic disorder caused by mutations in sarcomeric protein genes. The heart muscle thickens, potentially obstructing blood flow and impairing heart function. Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC): An electrical disturbance where heart muscle is replaced by fibrous scar tissue, primarily affecting the right ventricle. Restrictive Cardiomyopathy (RCM): The least common type, where the ventricular walls are stiff but not necessarily thickened, impeding normal blood filling. Noncompaction Cardiomyopathy: A congenital condition where the left ventricular wall fails to develop properly, resulting in a spongy appearance on echocardiography. Cardiovascular Disease Cardiovascular disease encompasses conditions affecting the heart and blood vessel system, including veins and arteries. Research indicates that women with cardiovascular disease often experience forms affecting blood vessels, while men are more likely to have conditions involving the heart muscle. Known causes include diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperhomocysteinemia, and hypercholesterolemia. Studies suggest that a low-fat, vegetarian diet can reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and may even reverse conditions like blood vessel restriction. Types include: Atherosclerosis Congenital Heart Disease Congenital heart disease refers to heart conditions present at birth, often due to unavoidable genetic factors. Examples include: Aortic Valve Stenosis Coronary Heart Disease Coronary heart disease results from the accumulation of atheromatous plaques in the walls of arteries supplying the myocardium. Symptoms and conditions include: Angina Pectoris and Myocardial Infarction (Heart Attack) Ischemic Heart Disease: Characterized by reduced blood supply to the heart. Heart Failure Heart failure, also known as congestive heart failure (CHF) or congestive cardiac failure (CCF), occurs when structural or functional cardiac disorders impair the heart's ability to fill with or pump sufficient blood. A specific type is: Cor Pulmonale: Failure of the right side of the heart. Hypertensive Heart Disease Hypertensive heart disease is caused by high blood pressure, particularly localized hypertension. Conditions include: Left ventricular hypertrophy Coronary heart disease (Congestive) heart failure Hypertensive cardiomyopathy Cardiac arrhythmias Inflammatory Heart Disease Inflammatory heart disease involves inflammation of the heart muscle or surrounding tissues. Types include: Endocarditis: Inflammation of the endocardium, often affecting heart valves. Inflammatory Cardiomyopathy Myocarditis: Inflammation of the myocardium, typically due to viral or bacterial infection. Symptoms may include chest pain, rapid onset of heart failure, or sudden death. Valvular Heart Disease Valvular heart disease involves any disease process affecting one or more heart valves. The valves on the right side of the heart are the tricuspid and pulmonic valves, while the left side contains the mitral and aortic valves.
